title: Caraka Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: The teaching of Punarvasu Ātreya set down by his disciple Agniveśa, redacted (pratisaṃskṛta) by Caraka and completed by Dṛḍhabala of Pañcanada, who supplied seventeen chapters of the Cikitsā and the Kalpa and Siddhi sections (Ca Si 12.36-40); Caraka is a partial incarnation of Śeṣa (Bhāvaprakāśa).
attribution.scholarly: A layered text: an older Agniveśa core, Caraka's redaction and Dṛḍhabala's supplement (c. 4th–5th c. CE).

tradition.text: Ātreya's teaching at the assembly of sages in the Himalaya, in a former age

scholarly.text: Caraka's redaction c. 1st c. BCE – 2nd c. CE; Dṛḍhabala c. 4th–5th c. CE

structure.description: Eight sthānas, 120 chapters (Ca Sū 30.33): Sūtra/Śloka 30, Nidāna 8, Vimāna 8, Śārīra 8, Indriya 12, Cikitsā 30, Kalpa 12, Siddhi 12

summary: The foundational compendium of internal medicine: Ātreya's teaching to Agniveśa in dialogues and assemblies of sages. It sets out the aim and definition of Āyurveda, the doṣas, dhātus and malas, diet, daily and seasonal routine and good conduct, the causes and diagnosis of disease, the examination of patient and physician, debate, the person and its constituents, embryology, the signs of death, therapeutics including rejuvenation and virility, and purificatory therapies; and it teaches a doctrine of the self, rebirth, yoga and liberation (Sū 11; Śā 1, 5).

editions.name: ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya with Cakrapāṇi's Āyurvedadīpikā (Bombay, Nirnaya Sagar 1941 and reprints)

notes: Refs in this unit: sthāna abbreviation + chapter.verse (su = Sūtra, ni = Nidāna, vi = Vimāna, sa = Śārīra, in = Indriya, ci = Cikitsā, ka = Kalpa, si = Siddhi); Ci 1 has four pādas (ci.1.4.30 = Cikitsā 1, pāda 4, verse 30).

title: Agniveśa Tantra
summary: The first tantra composed by a disciple of Ātreya (Ca Sū 1.32); survives only as redacted by Caraka and Dṛḍhabala in the Caraka Saṃhitā.

title: Bhela Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: Composed by Bhela, a fellow disciple of Agniveśa under Ātreya (Ca Sū 1.31-33).
attribution.scholarly: Extant in a single incomplete manuscript (Thanjavur); its relation to the original Bhela tantra is uncertain.

structure.description: Parallels the Caraka Saṃhitā's eight sthānas; many lacunae

summary: The only surviving compendium (partly) of another of Ātreya's disciples, closely parallel to Caraka in form. It locates manas between the head and the palate, supreme over the senses, and citta in the heart as the cause of all cognitions (Ci 8).

title: Hārīta Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: The tantra of Hārīta, disciple of Ātreya.
attribution.scholarly: The extant text is generally held to be a much later work bearing the old name.

summary: A medical compendium transmitted under the name of Ātreya's disciple Hārīta; the extant text is regarded by scholars as late.

title: Jatūkarṇa Saṃhitā
summary: The tantra of one of Ātreya's six disciples (Ca Sū 1.31-33); lost, known only through citations in later commentaries.
notes: Existence of the tantra is stated by Caraka; that citations survive is recalled, not checked.

title: Parāśara Saṃhitā (medical)
summary: The tantra of one of Ātreya's six disciples (Ca Sū 1.31-33); lost, known only through citations in later commentaries.
notes: Existence of the tantra is stated by Caraka; that citations survive is recalled, not checked.

title: Kṣārapāṇi Saṃhitā
summary: The tantra of one of Ātreya's six disciples (Ca Sū 1.31-33); lost, known only through citations in later commentaries.
notes: Existence of the tantra is stated by Caraka; that citations survive is recalled, not checked.

title: Suśruta Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: Dhanvantari, born as King Divodāsa of Kāśī, taught Suśruta and his fellow students (Su Sū 1.3-21); Ḍalhaṇa reports that Nāgārjuna redacted the text.
attribution.scholarly: Compiled in layers; the Uttaratantra is a later supplement; final form before c. 6th c. CE.

scholarly.text: core perhaps c. 2nd c. BCE onward; final redaction c. 3rd–6th c. CE

structure.description: Five sthānas of 120 chapters (Sūtra 46, Nidāna 16, Śārīra 10, Cikitsā 40, Kalpa 8) plus the Uttaratantra (66 chapters) — Su Sū 1.39-40

summary: The foundational compendium of the surgeons' school: the origin and eight limbs of Āyurveda, surgery and its instruments, the doṣas, dhātus and malas and the definition of health (Sū 15.41), the stages of disease (Sū 21), a Sāṃkhya account of creation and of the person (Śā 1), embryology, anatomy and the 107 marmas (Śā 6), therapeutics, rejuvenation, toxicology, and in the Uttaratantra eye, ear and head diseases, children's diseases, the seizing spirits (Utt 60) and the devices of exposition (Utt 65).

editions.name: ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya with Ḍalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṃgraha (Bombay 1938 and reprints)

title: Aṣṭāṅga Hṛdaya

attribution.tradition: Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta, 'lord of physicians' (colophons), who drew the essence from the tantras of Agniveśa and the others (Sū 1.3-5; Utt 40.80).
attribution.scholarly: c. 600 CE, Sindh; Buddhist affiliation argued from the opening salutation and the ten sinful acts (Sū 2.21-22); translated into Tibetan (Tengyur).

structure.description: Six sthānas, 120 chapters: Sūtra 30, Śārīra 6, Nidāna 16, Cikitsita 22, Kalpasiddhi 6, Uttara 40

summary: The most widely studied compendium, a verse synthesis of Caraka and Suśruta covering all eight limbs: the doṣas and their five-fold divisions (Sū 12), daily and seasonal routine and conduct (Sū 2-3), urges (Sū 4), diagnosis, therapeutics, surgery, rejuvenation (Utt 39) and virility (Utt 40). It opens with a salutation to the 'unprecedented physician' who destroyed the diseases of passion and the rest, and closes by urging impartiality: accept what is well said, whoever says it (Utt 40.86-88).

title: Aṣṭāṅga Saṅgraha

attribution.tradition: By Vāgbhaṭa (some later authors distinguish an elder Vāgbhaṭa, Vṛddha Vāgbhaṭa).
attribution.scholarly: Prose-and-verse compendium closely related to the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya; whether by the same author is debated.

structure.description: Six sthānas (Sūtra, Śārīra, Nidāna, Cikitsā, Kalpa, Uttara); c. 150 chapters

summary: The longer prose-and-verse compendium of the eight limbs from which (or alongside which) the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya was made; commented on by Indu (Śaśilekhā).
notes: Chapter count recalled (Sū 40, Śā 12, Ni 16, Ci 24, Ka 8, Utt 50) — not checked.

title: Mādhava Nidāna

structure.description: c. 60–70 chapters by disease, depending on the edition's division (the local e-text has 59)

summary: The standard diagnostic manual, compiled from the sayings of many sages (1.2): the five means of knowing a disease — cause, prodrome, manifest signs, response to trial therapy and pathogenesis (1.4) — then disease by disease.

title: Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā
summary: A concise handbook of pharmacy and therapeutics: weights and measures, pulse examination (nāḍī-parīkṣā, Pūrva 3), the functions of the body and of prāṇa (Pūrva 5), the forms of medicines, and mercurial and metallic preparations taken into Āyurveda from Rasa Śāstra.
notes: Distinct text from the anthology src:sarngadhara-paddhati; identity of the two Śārṅgadharas is debated.

title: Bhāvaprakāśa

structure.description: Three khaṇḍas (Pūrva, Madhya, Uttara); the Pūrva includes the origin of Āyurveda, embryology, daily routine and the drug lexicon (Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu)

summary: A late comprehensive compendium: the descent of Āyurveda (Brahmā, Dakṣa, the Aśvins, Indra; Ātreya and Bharadvāja; Caraka as a portion of Śeṣa; Dhanvantari born as Divodāsa), anatomy, regimen, a large materia medica, and therapeutics including newly described diseases.

title: Kāśyapa Saṃhitā

attribution.tradition: Mārīca Kaśyapa's teaching to Vṛddha Jīvaka, restored by Vātsya.
attribution.scholarly: Known from one fragmentary Nepalese manuscript, published 1938.

structure.description: Sthānas on the pattern of Caraka plus a Khilasthāna; large parts lost

summary: The principal classical text of the branch of children's medicine (kaumārabhṛtya): care of infant and wet-nurse, children's diseases, the seizing spirits of children (the Revatī chapter), and preparations for infants.

title: Āyurvedadīpikā
summary: Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā (11th c.); the standard commentary. Its opening salutes the lord of serpents who removed the faults of mind, speech and body through the Pātañjala, the Mahābhāṣya and the redaction of Caraka.

title: Bhānumatī
summary: Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary on the Suśruta Saṃhitā; only the Sūtrasthāna portion is known to survive.

title: Nibandhasaṅgraha
summary: Ḍalhaṇa's commentary on the Suśruta Saṃhitā (12th c.), the standard commentary; it reports Nāgārjuna as the text's redactor.

title: Nyāyacandrikā (Pañjikā)
summary: Gayadāsa's commentary on the Suśruta Saṃhitā, extant for the Nidānasthāna; used by Ḍalhaṇa.

title: Sarvāṅgasundarā
summary: Aruṇadatta's commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (13th c.).

title: Āyurvedarasāyana
summary: Hemādri's commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (13th c.).

title: Śaśilekhā
summary: Indu's commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha.

title: Nirantarapadavyākhyā
summary: Jejjaṭa's commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā, partly extant; among the earliest surviving commentaries.

title: Carakanyāsa
summary: Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra's early commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā, known from fragments and citations.

title: Madhukośa
summary: The commentary on the Mādhava Nidāna begun by Vijayarakṣita and completed by his pupil Śrīkaṇṭhadatta.

title: Carakatattvapradīpikā
summary: Śivadāsa Sena's commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā (15th c.).

title: Jalpakalpataru
summary: Gaṅgādhara Kaviratna's 19th-century commentary on the Caraka Saṃhitā, with his own recension of the text.

title: Dīpikā (on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā)
summary: Āḍhamalla's commentary on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā.

title: Gūḍhārthadīpikā (on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā)
summary: Kāśīrāma Vaidya's commentary on the Śārṅgadhara Saṃhitā.

title: Cakradatta (Cikitsāsaṅgraha)
summary: A therapeutic compendium by Cakrapāṇidatta, arranged by disease, much used in Bengal.

title: Siddhayoga (Vṛndamādhava)
summary: Vṛnda's collection of tried formulations arranged on the order of the Mādhava Nidāna.

title: Cikitsākalikā
summary: Tīsaṭa's short verse manual of therapeutics.

title: Cikitsāsārasaṅgraha of Vaṅgasena
summary: A large therapeutic compendium.

title: Gadanigraha
summary: Soḍhala's compendium of formulations and therapeutics.

title: Yogaratnākara
summary: An anonymous late compendium of diagnosis and formulations (including mercurial ones).

title: Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī
summary: A late compendium of formulations, widely used in modern Āyurvedic pharmacy.
notes: Date and authorship recalled with low confidence; possibly post-1800 (then recent).

title: Vaidyajīvana
summary: Lolimbarāja's poetic manual of therapeutics.

title: Āyurvedaprakāśa
summary: Mādhava Upādhyāya's treatise on mercurial and mineral medicine.

title: Dhanvantari Nighaṇṭu
summary: A lexicon of medicinal substances attributed to Dhanvantari.

title: Rāja Nighaṇṭu
summary: Narahari Paṇḍita's large lexicon of medicinal substances.

title: Madanapāla Nighaṇṭu
summary: A lexicon of materia medica under the name of King Madanapāla.

title: Kaiyadeva Nighaṇṭu
summary: A lexicon of diet and materia medica.

title: Aṣṭāṅga Nighaṇṭu
summary: A glossary of plant names keyed to Vāgbhaṭa's compendium, attributed to a Vāhaṭa.

title: Nāḍīparīkṣā
summary: A short late treatise on pulse examination, attributed in its colophons to Kaṇāda.

title: Tantrayuktivicāra
summary: A treatise on the devices of exposition (tantrayukti) of the medical texts, by Nīlamegha.

title: Nāvanītaka (the medical part of the Bower manuscript)
summary: A collection of formulations found among the Bower manuscripts from Kucha (Central Asia), in a Buddhist setting; among the oldest medical manuscripts.
notes: Edited and published (Hoernle); digitization status not checked.

title: Siddhasāra
summary: Ravigupta's compendium of medicine, translated into Tibetan and other Central Asian languages.
notes: Ravigupta's Buddhist affiliation is a scholarly inference.

title: Kalyāṇakāraka
summary: Ugrāditya's Jain compendium of Āyurveda, which excludes meat, alcohol and honey from therapy.

title: Hastyāyurveda
summary: The elephant medicine of Pālakāpya, framed as his dialogue with King Romapāda.

title: Aśvavaidyaka
summary: Jayadatta's treatise on the medicine of horses.

title: Vṛkṣāyurveda
summary: Surapāla's treatise on the care and healing of trees.

title: Rasārṇava
summary: A Śaiva tantra in the form of a dialogue of Bhairava and the Goddess: jīvanmukti in a stable body, mercury as Śiva's seed, worship of the mercurial liṅga, the teacher and initiation, the laboratory, the processing of mercury and minerals, metal transmutation and finally the transformation of the body (dehavedha). RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasahṛdayatantra
summary: Govinda's treatise in 19 avabodhas that opens with the soteriology of mercury — liberation comes from knowledge, knowledge from practice, practice needs a stable body — and then treats the processing of mercury and its transformative power (vedha). RESTRICTED: summary only.

attribution.tradition: By Govinda Bhagavatpāda (so named in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha), whom the tradition counts among the rasa-siddhas.
attribution.scholarly: A Govinda of c. 10th–11th c.; his identity with Śaṅkara's teacher is not accepted by scholars.

title: Rasaratnākara
summary: Nityanātha's compendium in five sections — mercury (for physicians), the lord of mercury (for the sick), metallurgy (for alchemists), rejuvenation (for the aged) and mantra (for mantra-practitioners) (Rasa-khaṇḍa 1.3-6). It warns that impure mercury is poison and that a physician skilled in practice but ignorant of the śāstra is death in human form. RESTRICTED: summary and warnings only.

title: Rasaratnasamuccaya
summary: A systematic compendium of mercurial and mineral medicine by 'the son of Siṃhagupta' (1.9): the twenty-seven siddhas of rasa (1.2-5), the minerals, gems and metals, the qualities of teacher and disciple and the laboratory (6), the impurities of mercury (11), and mercurial therapeutics. RESTRICTED: summary and warnings only.

attribution.tradition: By Vāgbhaṭa, son of Siṃhagupta (the author named in 1.9 as 'son of Siṃhagupta', as is the author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya).
attribution.scholarly: A 13th–14th-c. compilation; identity with the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya's author is doubted.

title: Rasendracūḍāmaṇi
summary: Somadeva's compendium of mercurial and mineral processing and medicine. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasaprakāśasudhākara
summary: Yaśodhara's compendium of rasa medicine. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasendracintāmaṇi
summary: A compendium of mercurial medicine; authorship is given differently in different sources. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasamañjarī
summary: Śālinātha's handbook of mercurial and mineral formulations. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasendrasārasaṅgraha
summary: A popular late handbook of rasa medicine. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Ānandakanda
summary: A large Śaiva text combining mercurial alchemy, rejuvenation (kalpa) regimens and haṭha-yogic practices, framed as Bhairava's teaching. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasādhyāya
summary: A short rasa text attributed to Kaṅkālayogin, with a commentary by the Jain Merutuṅga. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasasaṃketakalikā
summary: A short handbook of rasa medicine attributed to Cāmuṇḍa. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasakāmadhenu
summary: A late compendium of rasa medicine. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasataraṅgiṇī
summary: A 20th-century textbook of rasa medicine used in modern Āyurvedic colleges. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Kākacaṇḍīśvarīmata
summary: An early Śaiva alchemical tantra; Kākacaṇḍīśvara is named among the rasa authorities in the Rasaratnasamuccaya (1.6). RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasendramaṅgala
summary: An alchemical work attributed to Nāgārjuna. RESTRICTED: summary only.

title: Rasopaniṣad
summary: A Śaiva alchemical text published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series. RESTRICTED: summary only.
notes: Existence recalled; author and date unknown to me.

title: Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha
summary: Lineage contribution (Rasa Śāstra): its ninth chapter, the Raseśvaradarśana, presents the rasa doctrine as a Māheśvara system — jīvanmukti through a body made stable by mercury, mercury and mica as the seeds of Śiva and Gaurī, the eighteen processings of mercury (named but not explained), dehavedha rather than gold as the aim, and yoga in the stable body leading to the vision of the light between the brows — quoting the Rasārṇava, the Rasahṛdaya and the Raseśvarasiddhānta.
notes: U30 contribution only: the Raseśvara chapter (ch. 9). Authorship and dating as given by the owning units.

title: Raseśvarasiddhānta
summary: A rasa work quoted in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha's Raseśvara chapter (e.g. on beings who attained jīvanmukti through a mercurial body); not known to survive independently.
